b: Mycotic infection of humans and animals caused by different fungi and actinomycetes.
Eumycotic mycetoma — caused by true fungi
Actinomycotic mycetoma — caused by Actinomycetes (bacteria-like organisms)

Distribution: Worldwide but most common in barefoot populations in tropical/subtropical regions. Endemic in Africa, India, Central and South America. Mainly affects feet — mycetoma pedis (Madura foot)
Involves cutaneous and subcutaneous tissue; may reach bone

b: Entry via traumatic inoculation — thorns, splinters into skin; usually the foot
Organism spreads locally through subcutaneous tissue
Forms granulomatous reaction with draining sinuses
Characteristic grains (compact colonies of organism) discharged through sinuses
Can invade bone causing osteolysis if untreated

qs.q: A 42-year-old male presents with a chronic, draining foot sinus discharging granules. Biopsy confirms actinomycotic mycetoma rather than eumycotic mycetoma. How does the primary medical management of this bacterial-origin infection differ from fungal mycetoma?
o: Demands high-dose systemic amphotericin B infusion
Responds well to prolonged antibacterial regimens
Needs primary combination therapy with oral azoles
qs.e: Actinomycotic mycetoma is caused by filamentous bacteria and responds to prolonged antibiotics such as sulfonamides, whereas eumycotic mycetoma is caused by true fungi and is notoriously resistant to medical therapy. Surgical amputation is typically reserved for advanced eumycotic cases.
qs.s: Mycoses: Superficial, Cutaneous & Systemic Fungal Infections: MCQs

qs.q: Yellow granules on macroscopic examination indicate which type of mycetoma?
qs.e: Actinomycetes produce yellow granules, whereas eumycetes give black or white granules. Candida and Aspergillus are not associated with mycetoma.
qs.s: Mycoses: Superficial, Cutaneous & Systemic Fungal Infections: MCQs

qs.q: Which staining method is used to visualize fungal elements in mycetoma?
qs.e: KOH with calcofluor white highlights fungal hyphae. Gram stain does not detect fungal structures.
qs.s: Mycoses: Superficial, Cutaneous & Systemic Fungal Infections: MCQs

qs.q: On which medium and temperature is mycetoma mould isolated?
qs.e: Sabouraud dextrose agar at room temperature supports mould growth. The other media are unsuitable for mould isolation.
qs.s: Mycoses: Superficial, Cutaneous & Systemic Fungal Infections: MCQs

qs.q: Eumycotic mycetoma is resistant to which of the following?
qs.e: Eumycotic organisms are not susceptible to antibacterial agents. Antifungals are required for treatment.
qs.s: Mycoses: Superficial, Cutaneous & Systemic Fungal Infections: MCQs

qs.q: Actinomycotic mycetoma responds to prolonged therapy with which agents?
qs.e: Actinomycetes are treated with sulfonamides and streptomycin. Antifungals are ineffective against bacteria.
qs.s: Mycoses: Superficial, Cutaneous & Systemic Fungal Infections: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following is responsible for causing mycosis of the foot and is also associated with mycetoma in the Indian subcontinent?
o: Nocardia species, actinomycete bacteria causing actinomycetoma.
Madurella species, primary fungal agents of eumycetoma (Madura foot).
Fusarium species, common plant pathogens occasionally causing human infection.
qs.e: *Madurella mycetomatis* is a primary cause of Eumycetoma (fungal mycetoma) of the foot in the Indian subcontinent. *Nocardia* causes actinomycetoma.

ai.title: Mycetoma
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Mycetoma is a chronic subcutaneous infection of the foot caused by actinomycetes or true fungi, presenting with painless swelling, draining sinuses and characteristic grains. Diagnosis relies on clinical picture and grain microscopy; treatment is prolonged antimicrobial or antifungal therapy.

sections.p: Mycetoma is a chronic, granulomatous infection of skin and subcutaneous tissue, most often affecting the foot in barefoot tropical populations. It progresses slowly, forming painless swelling, multiple sinuses and discharge of coloured grains.

Two main groups: actinomycetes (e.g., Nocardia, Streptomyces) and true fungi (e.g., Madurella mycetomatis). Both form compact colonies (grains) that are visible in discharge and can be seen on microscopy.
b: Actinomycetes: gram‑positive, branching filaments, partially acid‑fast
Fungi: septate hyphae, produce pigmented grains

t.b: Identify organism type and guide therapy; actinomycotic grains are white/cream, fungal grains are brown/black

sections.p: Acquired by traumatic inoculation of soil or plant material through thorns or splinters. The organism multiplies locally, forming granulomas and sinuses; it may spread to bone.
Mycetoma is a chronic, destructive infection that can lead to deformity, disability and, if untreated, systemic spread. Bone involvement occurs in up to 50% of cases.

t.b: Shows soft tissue mass and bone erosion

sections.p: Clinical diagnosis is based on the triad of swelling, sinuses and grains. Confirmation requires grain microscopy or culture. In low‑resource settings, a simple Gram stain of grains is often used.

Actinomycotic mycetoma responds to long‑term antibiotics (e.g., trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole, amikacin). Eumycotic mycetoma requires prolonged antifungals (e.g., itraconazole, terbinafine). Surgery is reserved for refractory or extensive disease.
b: Surgical debridement if medical therapy fails

sections.p: Remember the classic triad and the importance of grain microscopy. In low‑resource settings, a simple Gram stain can guide therapy. Bone involvement warrants imaging and may change treatment duration.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly enlarging swelling, systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss), or new neurological deficits

faq.q: What is the most common site of mycetoma?
faq.a: The foot, especially the toes and heel, due to barefoot walking in endemic areas.

faq.q: How long does treatment usually last?
faq.a: 6–12 months for actinomycotic mycetoma; 12–24 months for eumycotic mycetoma, depending on response and bone involvement.
Use footwear, avoid barefoot contact with soil, and treat minor skin injuries promptly.
